speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: INLAND GAS PIPE LINE
subsubtopic: REPORTED EMPLOYMENT OF U.S. CITIZENS
speechtext:
May I ask the
Minister of Citizenship and Immigration or the Minister of Labour a question of which I have given both hon. gentlemen notice? Have either of the departments received complaints from western Canada regarding employment in the course of construction of the Inland Natural Gas pipe line to the effect that priority or preference seems to be given to United States employees crossing the border at Osoyoos, thus denying employment opportunities to Canadians?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Pickersgill (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration):
subtopic: INLAND GAS PIPE LINE
subsubtopic: REPORTED EMPLOYMENT OF U.S. CITIZENS
speechtext:
When the hon. gentleman first intimated that he intended to ask this question I had inquiries made in British Columbia and I found that there was no record there of any complaints having been made in the Vancouver office though there may have been at local offices of the employment service.
There are, I am informed, ten United States citizens employed in Canada by this company. Four are here with their families and have been landed as immigrants. Therefore they are, of course, entitled to be employed. Six are here under temporary status for six months, two engaged as distribution superintendents, two as spread superintendents and two as right of way foremen. In every case these workers were cleared by the national employment service as essential to the pipe line project before entry was authorized. In addition, there are at present applications by this company for the entry of one welding foreman and one pipe foreman awaiting clearance by the national employment service.
It has been suggested to me that it is conceivable that there might be United States citizens who had come in here as visitors and who had been hired by this company. Neither department has any knowledge of any such people. A check is being made, but if the

hon. gentleman or those who prompted his question have any knowledge of any such persons we would be very glad to have the information.

General items of payroll costs including superannuation payments-
561. To authorize and provide for a special government contribution to reduce the unamortized portion of the civil service superannuation account liability, $50,000,000.

Mr. Chairman, this item represents $50 million out of a total of $89.9 million in the further supplementary estimates and therefore it considerably outweighs in amount all the other items which are now engaging the attention of the committee. This item is unlike any other item in these further supplementary estimates because it does not contemplate a payment out of pocket on the part of the government. All the other items, with the exception of one kindred item of $50 million for losses on the realization of active assets, represent payments to be made but this item represents only a transfer from one pocket of the government to another. It does not represent an expenditure in the true sense of the word. These two items of $50 million each have been aptly described by one journalist when commenting upon some of the statements of recent days as amounts placed by the Minister of Finance in "piggy banks".
I have something to say about this item and the use which the government is endeavouring to make of it. If there is a case at all for putting money in the civil service superannuation fund to reduce what may be described in a loose sense as an actuarial deficit then the case is one for conscious budgeting on the part of the Minister of Finance in his annual estimates. This is not something that should be used by the government for the purpose of reducing its embarrassingly large surplus, which is the measure of the government's over-taxation of the people of Canada.
This matter of the civil service superannuation account for our purposes dates from 1947 when the act was revised by chapter 54 of the statutes of 1947. At that time certain revisions were made in the Civil Service Superannuation Act affecting this account. There previously had been no need for an accounting entry to reflect the so-called actuarial condition of the fund, but after the legislation of 1947 the government set up a paper account which was simply a ledger item in the consolidated revenue fund. Whatever amounts have been credited to that fund since have simply been amounts retained by the government in the consolidated revenue fund. They have never gone out of

Supply-Finance
the possession of the government. That is why I stress the fact that this item of $50 million is a non-cash transaction entirely within government accounts. It has no effect whatever on the cash surplus, but it does serve the purpose of the government in reducing the budgetary surplus by $50 million.
After this paper account was set up following the legislation of 1947 the department of insurance was instructed to make a study of the account. That department brought to the government a report which was completed in 1951 and tabled in 1952, the gist of which was that there was an actuarial deficit in the fund of $252 million as at December 31, 1947, and that as of December 31, 1951, the deficit amounted to $312 million.
Now, sir, lest anyone be too deeply impressed by references to an actuarial deficit, let us be quite clear on this: that an actuarial deficit in this sense in the case of private business and an actuarial deficit in this sense in the case of government business are two very different matters. In the case of the government dealing with a sovereign parliament, it rests within the power of parliament year by year on the recommendation of His Excellency to provide whatever is required regardless of a deficit or anything else. We are not dealing with a closed account as would be the case if this were a private business. It is not a serious matter that there should be a paper deficit in this fund. It is true that the account is credited with interest at 4 per cent per annum, but again this merely amounts to a bookkeeping entry, a paper entry within the scope of the government accounts.
After the report was brought in, and, indeed, in the year when the department of insurance was studying the position of the accounts, the government in further supplementary estimates proposed that a sum of money be credited to the account, and that practice has been followed now on three occasions. For the fiscal year 1950-51 a further supplementary estimate, item 587, for $75 million was passed and credited to this fund; in the fiscal year 1951-52, two items in the further supplementary estimates- No. 585 for $23 million and No. 586 for $75 million-were proposed and passed, and the sums credited to the fund. And in the fiscal year 1952-53, in the further supplementary estimates, by item No. 571, the sum of $25 million was similarly credited to this fund. In other words, in those three years a total of $198 million was taken out of the apparent government surplus as the end of the fiscal year approached, and credited to this fund.
I stress, sir, that in no case did the Minister of Finance at that time budget for that 
amount. In the dying days of the fiscal year the amount was taken out of the surplus in order to reduce the apparent budgetary surplus and to relieve the government of the embarrassment of an unwarranted huge surplus which did, in each case, represent the extent of government over-taxation of the people. And now we have to have a repetition of the same act.
Mr. Chairman, since that vote in the dying days of the fiscal year 1952-53, neither the present Minister of Finance nor his predecessor brought forward any proposal in his budgets for the allocation of any sum of this kind. It evidently was not a matter which, in their view, required to be budgeted, and the condition of the account was not such as to require, evidently, a conscious appropriation of money to strengthen the account.
Sir, I put it before the house that the government has approached this, not on the basis of sound financing, not on the basis of doing what might be, and what was in 1952 put forward by the former minister as something requiring regular annual budgeting, but simply as a political manoeuvre to relieve itself of the embarrassment of a large surplus.
On March 28, 1952, the then minister of finance in a reference to the item of $75 million in the further supplementary estimates to be allocated to this fund said, at page 910 of Hansard:
We propose to continue the policy initiated by the vote of $75 million a year ago and to wipe out the accumulated deficit over a reasonable period.
That was a clear enough statement. If the fund were one that required to be strengthened, then it is an understandable policy. But, having been so stated, it was completely ignored by the government. At the time the then minister of finance was speaking, he was simply dealing with this on the basis of a further supplementary estimate. He did not introduce any such item in his regular estimates for the ensuing fiscal year, but again, in the dying days of that fiscal year 1952-53, he brought in a further supplementary item. And nowhere, from the time this policy was enunciated by the then minister of finance in March, 1952, until this present time has there been any attempt on the part of the government to budget consciously for the strengthening of this paper account.
Let us see what this manoeuvre actually is: it is a palpable attempt on the part of the government to reduce the budgetary surplus and thereby its own embarrassment over that surplus. Six days ago the Minister of Finance undertook to tell the house at page 2217 of Hansard, that "our expenditure"- that is, for the fiscal year which will end on

the 31st of this month-"will be about $4,867 million and our surplus about $282 million." And again, in further reference to the same matter, he said: "The budgetary surplus is about $282 million."
Sir, the true budgetary surplus is a great deal more than that. Taking this item and the other similar paper item that I mentioned earlier of $50 million for loss on realization of assets-taking these two items alone, the true budgetary surplus is $382 million. The Minister of Finance has it within his power to propose to the house in these dying days of this fiscal year that his budgetary surplus be reduced by these two figures aggregating $100 million, but at least he might have the grace to call this by its true name; he might at least have the grace to say that the true budgetary surplus is $382 million, but that the government proposes to cover up and hide $100 million of it, not by putting it out as expenditure but simply by retaining possession of these two sums of $50 million each and transferring them, always within the consolidated revenue fund, to the credit of a paper account. That is what is involved here, and it is no more than that. It is simply a political manoeuvre for which there is precedent on three occasions when the conditions were similar, namely when the Minister of Finance and the government having grievously over-taxed the people then sought to relieve themselves of the burden of accounting for a huge surplus by hiding part of it within the consolidated revenue fund by means of a paper entry.
It is not to be wondered at, Mr. Chairman, that this strategem is resorted to on the eve of an election.
I am sure that we can very well conclude that but for that fact and the government's embarrassment about this surplus there would be before us today no further supplementary estimate in regard to a matter like this. The minister has overtaxed the Canadian people. He does not want the people to realize the extent to which they have been overtaxed and consequently resort is had to methods of this kind to hide a substantial portion of the true budgetary surplus. Sir, the house should realize that it is being asked to take part in an act of hiding a substantial portion of the true budgetary surplus.

I should like to add a word to what my colleague has said. I shall be very brief. I have looked back to what was said by the minister's predecessor several years ago. At that time we were led to believe that this matter was going to be dealt with in a planned and regular manner. I think we are entitled to have that done.

Can anyone suggest that it is being done in that way? It is and has been done in a spasmodic, haphazard way which is related to nothing so far as we can see except, as my colleague has said, the desire of the minister to make his surplus look less than it really is on certain occasions.
When are those occasions? We know when they are when we look back. They are related to general elections and big surpluses. As my colleague has said, why do we have to have this make-believe? Why can we not have a budget related to the realities of the situation? The only real thing about this is that $50 million has been taken away from the taxpayers. That is real enough. When we get the true view we realize that $50 million added to another $50 million and added to $282 million makes $382 million.
I do not think I need pursue the matter at length, but I wish to make it clear that I agree fully with what my colleague has said. I hope the minister is going to say something about it. I think we are entitled to some word from him and that he should not leave it entirely unanswered because he knows as well as we do that these arguments are sound and that we are entitled to an answer. I certainly ask the minister not to let this thing go through without answering. If he does, it is just another instance of that attitude of superiority-I do not want to use unpleasant words to describe it-based on long occupation of the government benches and based on the feeling which each year apparently grows stronger that the answer to any question is, did we or did we not get elected?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: There is a question I wanted to put to the minister but I will defer if he wishes to answer the comments that have been made.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I suppose I should say something in view of the last two or three sentences of the hon. member for Greenwood which displayed a state of mind that I hoped really would not grow up in the house. We are sent here for the purpose of making our representations, making our speeches and explanations and saying those things that we feel we should say. But I have never thought that because one person says one thing someone else is bound to say something else. Indeed, it seems to me that occasionally one would be wise not to say some of the things I have heard said in the house.
But having in mind that my hon. friend feels it would be unfair to him or, at any rate, I would be unfair to myself if I did not answer, in other words, that I would be under the stigma he has put on me of supposing I am superior, which I never do and he

Supply-Finance
knows I do not, I will make an answer. We seem to be proceeding on the assumption that because the government asks for this vote of $50 million towards the end of the fiscal year this is somehow coming out of the taxpayers whereas it would not if we had asked for it at the beginning. If we had budgeted for this the result would have been precisely the same. We would have had the same tax rate, we would have collected the same amount of revenue-I am speaking generally of course-and the money would have been transferred in the consolidated revenue fund to the superannuation account.
Therefore when the hon. member for Eglinton and the hon. member for Greenwood suggest there would have been any other result than the result we are now going to achieve it seems to me they have overlooked the fact that it would have been in the blue book in the first place and would have been subject to debate just as this item is now subject to debate, but the result would have been just the same if the vote had carried in the long run. With regard to the government doing nothing about these things since 1952-53 and only using the opportunity which arises when a budgetary surplus is available, I think the committee ought to know that after the study was made in 1948-49 and following on the statements made by my predecessor in 1949 and again in 1952 the government has done something about this every year.
When civil service salaries are increased we have a statutory provision now which we did not have at that time that the appropriate amount that has to go into this account has to be voted, and we did that last year. When we raised the salaries of the civil servants and the armed forces my recollection is that the increases ran to about $40 million or something of that order and an amount precisely the same as the expected increase was voted by the house and put in this account to make sure that the account did not go further into the red. Also from year to year when civil servants elect to pay their contributions on certain service which they have already built up but with respect to which they have not been entitled to contribute because they had not become permanent or for some other reason, the government then matches that particular contribution for a period back beyond the date when the civil servant first elects to make his contribution. In the meantime and in addition we have been paying the interest on this account ever since the particular report was made by my predecessor.
Therefore since 1948 or 1949 the account has not gone into arrears at any time, and instead of there being a deficit of $509 mil-

lion, as was reported by the committee that looked into the matter at that time, we now have a deficit of $189 million, and if this vote is approved the deficit will be $139 million. I can only say that if my hon. friends take any comfort out of the fact that there seems to be a coincidence between the use of large surpluses for this purpose and non-budgeting on other occasions I should think the very reasons that prompt them to speak as they have are reasons why we would not budget in that way in a year when revenues may not be as buoyant and we may not have the margin of funds that we need, and that it would be on an occasion like this when we can use the surplus that should be used in order to reduce the deficit until in due course there will be no deficit at all. When we get the fund down to the point of being actuarily sound I do not know what my hon. friends will be able to say at that time when there is no large item such as this for them to use to say we have a large surplus. I only know that this government will likely be in power at that time and that we will do what we think ought to be done at that time.

Mr. Chairman, the minister has sought to brush this matter aside rather lightly in his explanation of the net result. But the house should not be so easily led as to think that this matter is quite so simple. Had the minister consciously budgeted for the two items of $50 million which we have been discussing he would not have announced in his budget speech a year ago that he was budgeting for a surplus of $113 million. He would have announced that he was budgeting for a surplus of $13 million, a very different matter. The people of the country would then have been in a position to compare his $282 million against his estimated $13 million, whereas today they will have the opportunity of comparing the $382 million of correct budgetary surplus against his estimate of $113 million. There are other factors involved in this comparison as well.
The minister has had full opportunity today, if he seriously believes in the policy of eliminating this paper deficit, to announce a policy; to announce that he intends in future to budget consciously and to ask the house to approve a deliberate policy of elimination of this paper deficit. But he has chosen not to make use of that opportunity. I call upon him to announce-if he believes in it-a definite long-range policy setting forth the rate at which this paper or actuarial deficit will be reduced annually until it is eliminated. In that way we shall prevent the government from using this actuarial deficit in its accounts as a means of concealing the true dimensions of its budgetary

surplus in years like the present one when it has so grievously overtaxed the Canadian people.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: May I ask the minister whether it would make any difference at all to recipients of pensions out of this fund whether this money were paid over or were not paid over at the present time?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No. The government is obliged to honour its obligations to the civil servants upon retirement and the pensions will be paid in full whether or not these funds were voted in this way.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: May I ask one other question? Would it be possible to put money of this kind into the fund to make it possible to pay higher pensions to those already retired, particularly those whose pensions are in the lower brackets?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: If the government concludes that it ought to pay higher pensions to retired civil servants, I presume that it would be necessary to present that as a policy and to seek a vote of the house for that specific purpose. That vote, if carried, would of course transfer the money into this fund.
Item agreed to.
551. Estimated amount required to recoup the agricultural prices support account to cover the net operating loss of the agricultural prices support board during the fiscal year 1956-57, $5,019,100.

Mr. Chairman, on Monday we listened to the Minister of Agriculture tell us the various prices that are being paid for eggs at different points across the country, that the floor price or the so-called floor price under the Agricultural Prices Support Act for eggs was 38 cents a dozen for grade A large, and that from that price are deducted the costs of storage, handling charges and so on to get what is ordinarily considered the effective floor price of 32 cents a dozen.

May I just correct one statement. I think it is not quite correct to say that the amount of carrying charges, storage and so on is deducted. As a matter of fact, it is added and it comes out to 43 cents.

Then after all the other commissions, interest, carrying charges et cetera have been deducted, it comes to the producer, under the rough rule of thumb method used by the Minister of Agriculture, to a price of 32 cents a dozen. As I understand it, if 32 cents a dozen is being paid, then it is assumed that the purpose of the legislation is being carried out. But although this act has done some considerable good and although even in recent months a great many eggs have been purchased under the act, I do not think
Supply-Agriculture
the producers are getting full value from the legislation and I do not think that the money the public of Canada are investing in the purchase and storage of eggs is in fact being adequately passed on to the producer.
I am amazed to find at times that the prices paid for eggs are so much below the 32 cents a dozen. I think that fact suggests that this whole act, under which the item in the estimates is being paid, should be overhauled. I do not think it is good enough to have on the statute books an act that does not bring full benefit to the producer. I think it is assumed by all members in the house, that under the constitution, the federal government has or can have control over prices of products going into interprovincial and export trade. There does not seem to be any question about that matter. It would seem to me that under this act the government should make certain that all eggs going into interprovincial trade have been purchased at the floor price. It may be difficult-I know it would be difficult-to make certain that every single dozen of eggs sold from person to person in the country carries the floor price. But certainly any firms that are doing business in interprovincial trade should be required to pay the floor price under this act. I think there is a method by which they can be required to pay the floor price.
We have another extremely important act that deals with an agricultural commodity in interprovincial and export trade. I refer of course to the Canadian Wheat Board Act. In order to make certain that the firms which are purchasing wheat and shipping wheat in interprovincial and export trade are in fact paying the prices set out by the Canadian Wheat Board, there is listed in the act a schedule of firms which act as agents of the board. I suggest that under the Agricultural Prices Support Act there should be a schedule of firms that can act as agents of the agricultural prices support board and that, in order to act as agents, they should be required to pay the floor price.
The minister has given the committee information to the effect that the floor price or the support price even recently has not been paid and that the places where the support price has not been paid and is not being paid today are in the prairie provinces mainly. We all know that in the province of Ontario in recent weeks many instances have been brought to our attention where the floor price is not being paid. The minister went on to attempt to criticize the government of Saskatchewan for not having built storage for eggs. As far as I know, the governments of the other provinces are not in the storage business. I have inquired. I am told by

Supply-Agriculture
Manitoba members that, to their knowledge, the Manitoba government is not building storage.
It is not a socialist government.

The Manitoba government is
not building storage and it is not a socialist government. The government of which the minister is a member, of course, is not a socialist government but it has been very closely associated with the business of building cold storage for all kinds of commodities. So this rion-socialist government is doing what the minister says a socialist government should do.
I am not saying what they should do. I am saying what they said they would do.

I do not expect they said
anything of the kind. The minister is always looking for an alibi. He will condemn the Saskatchewan government for not having done something even if the Manitoba government, a Liberal government of many years' standing, has never even considered doing the same thing. The amazing part of the list of prices that he put on the record is the fact that in Manitoba the price is as low as that at all of the Saskatchewan points he mentioned arid there is one point, namely Brandon, where the price being paid is even lower than the other prices that the minister has quoted.
I do not think you can have an act that is effective unless you attack the problem of storage. I do not think it can be attacked effectively by attempting to shoulder the responsibility on one provincial government. If any one provincial government built all the storage required for all the eggs that might be put into storage in that province, that would do nothing under this act to provide a floor price for egg producers in the other nine provinces. I believe the government should require the packing firm to pay the floor prices, as an agent of the agricultural prices support board, and the firms that have agreed to pay those prices should be made known. Then, the government should expand its policy of subsidizing the building of cold storage facilities to the point that the act may be effective and that producers may receive the support price.
I think if this were done it would probably save the consumer money. I imagine one of the reasons why egg prices become so high at particular times of the year is the fact that nothing has been done, or very little has been done, in periods of very high prices to effectively store eggs so that they may be available at a later date, even a few

days or a few weeks later as that often represents the difference between periods of high prices and low prices.
Another thing I suggest, and I think this is absolutely essential, is that the government set out a schedule of payments for the various grades. It is not good enough to have a suggested floor price for a certain grade and then have no price support at all for the other grades. Any legislation that is going to be effective must set out a schedule of grades, and have attached to each grade its appropriate floor price. We know that in the case of grade A medium eggs, very often the spread is enormous and unwarranted. I think this defect can be overcome by setting out floor prices for grade A medium eggs, and for any other grades that might be appropriate.
I suggest that the act should have some teeth in it. Firms should not be allowed to get away with chiselling the price for eggs down to very low points. Firms who are participating in the government program should be listed, and they should agree to pay the support price on all eggs that they purchase. If this were accompanied by appropriate penalties if the act were broken by these firms, I think you would find the packing houses passing on the floor prices to the producers. If the government would then take a look at the storage facilities in the country to ascertain whether or not it is necessary to expand this program of subsidizing cold storage construction, then I think we might have an effective act.
The Agricultural Prices Support Act as it is being applied to eggs, and as it has been applied to hog prices in the past, has very often failed to give to the producers the floor prices set out in the act. I want to point out in fairness that this is not true in the case of butter prices. We have felt that the floor price on butter has, almost without exception, been passed on to the producer. The same thing, of course, is true with regard to the initial prices established for grain under the Canadian Wheat Board Act. The effective policies that have been followed with regard to several agricultural commodities, I suggest, should be adopted and followed in connection with egg prices.

Mr. Chairman, the other evening I stated that there would be some announcement to be made with regard to certain milk prices, either yesterday or today. I just want to read that announcement now since it was only partly covered in that statement. I am quoting from the order in council which sets up the plan:
That under the authority of paragraph (b) of subsection (1) of section 9 of the Agricultural Prices Support Act, the agricultural prices support

board proposes to purchase Canada first grade dry skimmed milk and that under authority of paragraph (a) of the said subsection the board proposes to prescribe the following prices (f.o.b. storage at Moncton, Montreal, Toronto, Winnipeg, Regina, Edmonton, Vancouver) with all purchases of both spray and roller process dry skimmed milk to be subject to such terms and conditions as may be specified by the agricultural prices support board.
The prices set are 14 cents per pound for Canada first grade dry skim milk, roller process, and 17 cents per pound for Canada first grade dry skim milk, spray process.
The undersigned, therefore, has the honour to recommend as follows:
1.	That your excellency the governor general in council under the authority of paragraph (a) of section 2 of the Agricultural Prices Support Act, 1944, be pleased to designate as an agricultural product, for the purposes of the said act, Canada first grade dry skimmed milk.
2.	That your excellency the governor general in council be pleased to approve of the board prescribing the prices aforesaid for the purposes of paragraph (a) of subsection (1) of section 9 of the said act.
That is the plan which has been announced and which is to be followed in connection with dry milk powder.
I only wish to say a few words with regard to the remarks just made by the hon. member for Assiniboia. First, the plan which he outlined is approximately the plan which they had in the United States. It was the outcome of that plan which we were attempting to avoid when we set up our system some years after theirs had come into effect and after having seen the experience of their plan. Their plan was one which encouraged the production of eggs to the extent they filled all the storages in the country. I am sure hon, members recall that they even filled caves in the United States with eggs. After having had that experience, they had to change their policy. We set up our policy after that experience had been had in the United States.
The important fact is that after we had carried on under our policies and they under that policy and then the corrected one, our prices of eggs are just as high as in the United States, and most of the time higher. I think the outcome of our plan has proven that it is at least as acceptable as any that has been followed elsewhere.
In so far as the matter of cold storage is concerned, I did not imply nor say at any time it was the duty of any particular provincial government to build cold storage. I just referred to the fact that we have a particular kind of government in Saskatchewan which had undertaken to do those things. They were even going to build packing plants, and said so. It is the packing plants which do a considerable amount of this storage. They stated that; but then after
Supply-Agriculture
they got in no doubt they found it was not a thing they could practicably do and so they did not do it. But whatever the reason, the plants are not there, and you have a government in Saskatchewan which maintained it would be building that kind of plant when it got in.
My hon. friend says we do something similar. Well, we do pay one-third of the cost of all cold storage right across Canada wherever it is carried on in accordance with the act. Two storages have been put into Saskatchewan within the last three years, one in Regina and one in Saskatoon, on which we did pay one-third of the cost; and while these storages are not especially for the storage of eggs-probably you could not store eggs in them because they are freezing plants-they do take a considerable portion of the products out of other cold storages and leave room for certain other products and to an extent eggs. So this government has done something about the storage problem that exists there while, I suggest again, the provincial government in its own good judgment has done nothing about it.
Neither has any other provincial government.

The only difference it makes is that it does tend to reduce the price by about 2 cents, because the eggs have to be shipped to Winnipeg or Calgary and therefore the price level is down a little, but it does not make any more difference than that. On the other hand there are provinces in Canada where they eat all the eggs they produce. The problem really is not one that concerns anyone outside the province, any more than that some of the other provinces may want to ship eggs there.
For example, with regard to the province of Ontario, from which we have had cases cited, the eggs spoken of are laid by the hens of Ontario-
We expected that.
Hear, hear.

-produced in the hatcheries of Ontario. They are gathered up and taken into storage in Ontario, or they may be loaded on trucks and then taken into the city of Toronto and sold. We have nothing to do with those eggs. There is no law we could pass that would bring those eggs under our control. Those eggs are bought from a farmer. He makes his own deal with the purchaser and that person takes them into town-in the case I mentioned the other night, into the town of Lindsay-and they accumulate there. They are then moved from

Supply-Agriculture
Lindsay into Toronto, let us say, and sold to merchants in that city who in turn sell them to the public. We have nothing to do with those eggs at all. We cannot take any control over them.
On the other hand, however, the persons who are handling the eggs could put them under the act, and if they did they would become agents of the government. My hon. friends have stated that we ougth to have agents of the government. The Agricultural Prices Support Act provides for our appointing agents, and we do have agents to handle the products. When a certain set of conditions are established it becomes possible for a certain organization to be an agency of the government under that act. If they carry out the terms of the act they do become agents of the government.
One of those terms is that they must pay the farmers a reasonable price. No one has ever said that 32 cents is a reasonable price for eggs across this country. A reasonable price is a price that is properly related to the 38-cent floor at the storage plant to which they are delivered. The only charge that can be made against that 38 cents is the cost the individual company or corporation or whatever it is has in bringing those eggs from the producer to the plant. He is allowed a reasonable profit in connection with these transactions. All that is checked back before delivery of these eggs is taken under this act.
When we established the act originally it was not intended that eggs would be accepted until December. During the first two or three years no delivery was taken until then. Some of the experiences required that we give assurances at the time the eggs were put into storage that if the holder of the eggs desired to have them turned over to us at the first of December we would be prepared to take them.
We functioned in that way for another year or two but there were difficulties in that connection, and the regulations have been amended since that time to make it possible for us to buy eggs at any time, to actually take delivery of them and pay for them and see that they are put in cold storage. That does not necessarily mean we will take delivery of the eggs on the day on which we give the undertaking. It is done both ways.
If the person who has the eggs in cold storage under our direction desires to take them out of cold storage and sell them or distribute them as he sees fit, to his own advantage, he can do that; but if he carries them on through to a certain period in the year, then we take delivery of the eggs.

This plan was set up after consultation with the representatives of the producers' organizations. They were in Ottawa representing egg producers from all the provinces in Canada, as I recall it. At that time we discussed the matter together with those who are engaged in the storing of eggs and those involved in trade in connection with eggs. They held a meeting here in Ottawa. They came to us with a certain proposal somewhat along the lines outlined by my hon. friend a few moments ago.
We told them that in view of the experience in the United States we did not think we could make that work, and so we proposed a plan. We started out by accepting delivery of stored eggs on December 1 at 38 cents, with carrying charges added. If the eggs were put in storage in May there was a certain carrying charge, and if they were put in storage in August there was also a carrying charge, and so on. The limit that could be charged under the act for carrying charges as it then read was 5 cents, and so the eggs could run up in value to about 42 or 43 cents, and that is the price at which we actually took them.
That plan operated for one year, and then the same group came back. The gentleman who was at the head of the group-incidentally, he came from Winnipeg-came to us before the others had congregated and suggested that he still thought the plan advanced the year before was the right one. They held their meeting and they came back to see us. The gentleman got up and apologized for having taken the position he took, and advised us that the others agreed with him and were now unanimously in favour of continuing the plan that was in effect the year before. They meet annually and give us their opinions every year.
The advisory committee which is representative of all the provincial farm organizations and provinces across Canada meets twice every year and we talk about this matter. I am not going to say what the advisory committee does because that is a behind closed doors meeting, and we do not discuss their opinions; but they do discuss it every year and comment upon it. The federation of agriculture also meets from time to time and passes resolutions about these things, and there has been no undue criticism of the system itself.
People question why eggs sell at such low prices. All I am saying is that most of the eggs that are sold at low prices and about which we talk a great deal out in the country have never been graded at all. They are the nest run of eggs, eggs that are brought in from places where there are no proper grading stations to take care of their grading.

On the other hand, in some provinces you will find egg grading stations located in many places, wherever eggs are produced. As far as I am aware the egg grading situation in Ontario is pretty well covered and stations have been located there for a long time, but the situation is different in my province, as everyone from Saskatchewan knows, where you have to do some hunting to find an egg grading station.
This may be true because there is no great demand for them. In any case they are not there, and so the eggs that are produced in those areas come in quantities that are not graded and cannot be brought under this or any other act that could be passed here. The act provides for graded eggs. The hon. member has suggested that probably the plan could be amended to take care of the extra large, grade A large and medium. Probably we could go that far without any change in the act, and we do consider from time to time the advisability of making it apply in that way.
I would say that at the present there is only one thing that would happen if we made it apply, and that is it would lower the price of eggs to those who produce medium grade. The reasonable margin as between the two is about 5 cents, and I noted that the margin this morning was about 1 cent. For weeks past the margin has been 2 cents, so if we were to put on what is called a reasonable margin as between grade A large and the mediums we would probably reduce the price to the producer of medium eggs.
It is easy to understand why at the moment the price of medium eggs is high as compared to grade A large. Pullets are not laying eggs at the present time and of course medium eggs practically all come from pullets, the new layers. Large eggs come from older hens, and right at this time the medium supply is low, because the number of pullets is low at this time. If we set a margin of 5 cents we would probably take away some of the price which the producer of medium eggs now gets.
All these things are considered regularly. One difficulty about eggs is that they are a perishable product. You can crack them taking them into town, and you can do all kinds of things with eggs that will not happen to potatoes or apples or other things. I suggest that it is easy enough to talk about it but it is not quite so easy to carry it out. We must have the absolute co-operation of the provincial governments with all the legislation they can give. My hon. friend is anxious to talk about amendments to the marketing legislation and we are told the provinces are asking for this now, and
Supply-Agriculture
the province of Ontario particularly are urging us to give them co-operation by passing legislation here.
Why not?
We say we are quite prepared to do it and our intention is to do it, but I think it is just as reasonable for us to say that the provinces should give us all the legislation we require.
Have you asked them for it?

We have asked them a dozen times. I have asked them out in my hon. friend's province, and I will ask them again. I do not know whether they will do it, but we will continue to ask for it. I would suggest that it is just as important that the provinces co-operate with us in giving us the necessary legislation to do these things as it is that we should co-operate with them. That is all we ask the Saskatchewan government or any other government to do. We get more co-operation from some than we do from others.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: About a month ago pressure was being applied on the government and on the opposition, and in turn the opposition was putting more pressure on the government. Why did the government have to wait until that pressure was applied before they took action?

Pressure had nothing to do with it. If you can tell me why the hatcheries prefer to have eggs produced at a certain time then I will answer you. The fact is that eggs produced from about the middle of November, certainly from the 1st of December down to the 1st of February, are not suitable for oil-dipping. The feeding of the hens and the care given them and everything else reduces the quality of those eggs, and the only time you can start profitably to put on oiling is around February 1. The producers of eggs know that, and those who are engaged in the marketing of eggs know that. If you have a large production of eggs then that is the time when somebody can get cheap eggs. They may not all be the best, but they will be cheaper.
There is not much we can do about it. That is one of the difficulties of carrying on a plan of this kind unless you have everybody's co-operation. Immediately we get to the time when we are certain that those eggs will keep for at least until July 1, so we will have some opportunity of putting them on the market as shelled eggs, we will take the eggs and oil-dip them ourselves. This was done after January 26.

There is one matter that should be cleared up. The hon. member for

Supply-Agriculture
Assiniboia mentioned a price to the producer of 32 cents a dozen. I was under the impression that the carrying or servicing charge, which had previously been 6 cents, had been increased to 8 cents early this year. How you can take 8 cents from 38 cents and still have 32 cents left I do not know. I would like the minister to tell us whether that is true.
The minister made reference to eggs going into Lindsay, and he said they had no control over them. But in the next breath he said they could still come under this floor even though they had no control over them. In that case the eggs were being marketed within the province, but the minister was saying they could come under the control of this floor price. I do not know how that is possible, but the minister has said that dealers had to pay a certain price or the government would not guarantee the 38-cent floor.

What I said was that if they do not conform with certain requirements the government will not take their eggs at 38 cents any time. They know and understand that. If they have any desire to turn their eggs over to the government they buy them under the conditions set out in the understandings they have.
With regard to the other question, I am sorry I have not the regulation here. As reported a few minutes ago, the first regulation set the price at 38 cents plus the maximum carrying charge of 5 cents. That is what we undertook to pay. I am speaking from memory, but I believe that has been raised 1 cent recently because the carrying charges now are a little higher than they were at that time. But the carrying charge is not included in the 38 cents. You can say that to anyone who indicates to you that that carrying charge would bring the price down to 32 cents.
The only thing that would bring it down to 32 cents is the cost of accumulating a carload of eggs or a truckload of eggs in order to ship in to a certain point. They bring in those eggs in those quantities and deliver them to the storage. The government will accept them if the eggs are properly graded and so on, and the producer will receive a reasonably related price. That means that if they have brought them in from 300 miles away there will be a wider margin than there will be if they are brought in from only 100 miles away, or possibly only 25 miles away.
There is no one price that you can say is a reasonable price when you take all the circumstances into consideration. The board agrees to accept the eggs, and once they are put into storage under their acceptance we

are bound to take them at least by December 1. Sometimes we take them earlier and sometimes we leave them there. On some occasions when we have left them there they got rid of them before December 1 and we did not need to take anything. Our undertaking is that they get a floor price of 38 cents at the storage and also the carrying charges up to the time the eggs are taken out, if we take them the producer must have had a properly related price. In addition to that we must be assured that they paid a reasonable price for them at the time they got them from the producer.

On
Monday evening, Mr. Chairman, the minister put on record in Hansard some figures dealing with losses incurred in the handling of certain agricultural products. He pointed out that in 1955 the loss incurred in handling butter amounted to over $4 million, and that in 1956 it was more than $500,000. I would like to ask the minister if he could tell the committee how many pounds of butter were sold in Canada for less than the floor price of 58 cents to institutions and other concerns coming under the 21 cents a pound subsidy, and also how many pounds of butter were sold outside Canada and at what price.

I have a general statement on that which will, I think, answer most of the questions that have been asked. The last year for which I have figures on the statement from which I read two nights ago, is 1954, but I also have figures from 1949 to 1954; then in the annual report for 1955-1956, which I have here, there is a general statement which says this:	First
grade creamery butter produced in 1955, 62,990,606 pounds. That is the inventory as of March 31, 1956, held by the board. Then stock on hand, March 31, 1956, 54,712,239 pounds. That, of course, is in storage right across the country.
In addition to the other products to which we are giving support, the board considered further proposals mainly relating to the diversification of supports in the dairy industry, but up to March 31, 1956, no action was considered necessary except to continue to support the price of first grade creamery butter. First grade creamery butter, 1954-55 production, held as on March 31,	1955,
amounted to 50,190,509 pounds. This was all butter made in 1954. At the beginning of May, 1955, this butter was offered to the trade on the basis of 58 cents per pound less a handling charge for storage of 2 cents per pound. Approximately 10 million pounds were sold on this basis up to June 30, 1955. At that time the board ceased to offer 1954 production butter until the beginning of

August, 1955, at which time it offered and sold the remainder of the stocks of 1954 butter on the basis of 58 cents per pound, except for 9 million pounds which were exported. That is the answer to the question regarding the amount exported. It was approximately 9 million pounds.
With respect to these exports, the board had indicated in December, 1954, that it was willing to consider offers for export. In June, 1955, an experimental shipment of approximately 300,000 pounds of unsalted butter was sold by a Canadian trader for export. The price received by the board was approximately 37 cents f.a.s. Montreal. Further export deals in 1954 salted butter took place in the latter part of 1955 and early in 1956 at prices ranging from 37 cents to 39 cents f.a.s. Canadian seaboard. The total quantity involved was approximately 9 million pounds.
In February, 1955, the board offered to approved Canadian institutions a rebate or discount of 21 cents per pound on first grade creamery butter purchased by them. This program ran until March 31, 1956, at a cost of $1,427,930, representing discount and charges on about 6.7 million pounds. A study of these sales in February, 1956, as compared with the month prior to the entry of the institutions into the plan, based on the reports made by these institutions, showed that there had been an increase of approximately 9 per cent in the consumption of butter by these institutions during that period.
The total loss on 1954 butter sold by the board was $5,422,152.91, including $55,861.36 shown in the account up to March 31, 1955. The sum of $5,302,299.95 was included in the March supplementary, and a balance of $63,991.60 was carried forward into the current fiscal year.

Mr. Chairman, I think some hon. members may be more confused than ever, now, regarding these egg prices. It has been very unfair that according to the minister's statement there is no set figure which the producer can expect for his eggs or for the eggs being sold through dealers to the government-
There is a set figure which may be established in every community, but not one that applies all across Canada.

I understand there is not one that applies all across Canada. But let the minister give us some of the set figures allowed to dealers transporting these eggs to storage. Let him give us, now, the figure that will be permitted under this act to those dealers transporting eggs from various places into storage, so we may know what
Supply-Agriculture
the producer can expect. How can he know what he is supposed to expect for grade A large eggs if he does not know these figures?

Mr. Chairman, one would think to hear hon. members of the official opposition, particularly those who speak on this question-though I am quite sure they do not all agree-that this government ought to be in the business of the marketing of eggs and that we ought to be taking delivery of the eggs, checking everybody in order to see that they do nothing except what this government instructs them to do.	*
That is not the policy at all. The policy is that everyone who wishes to be in the egg business may stay in the egg business. This act is simply set up to make it possible for them to secure certain advantages for the producers if they wish to do so. But only a small percentage of the eggs really comes under the administration of this act; in some years, none at all. The act is on the statute books, and it indicates that if anyone cannot get 38 cents for eggs in storage, and they prefer to put them in storage on our account, we will take them. But there is one good reason why they don't let us get them. If a man is in the egg business he wants to be able to make his own deals and sell his own eggs. Once he puts them in our hands we can give them to a business competitor or to anyone else. So he does not put them in our hands at all unless he is satisfied that it will be to his advantage, or to the advantage of people associated with him, as producers to do so.
Hon. members of the C.C.F. party are quite prepared to criticize this kind of arrangement, but I cannot understand the official opposition criticizing it. We say to everyone, stay in the business and do business as you think you ought to do it. If you have any surplus that you cannot take care of at a price, bring it to us and we will pay the set price for it provided you have treated the producer fairly.
In most cases they do not come near us at all, and certainly when farmers accept 26 to 28 cents for eggs in the area between Toronto and Lindsay the dealer will not bring the eggs to the support board. The farmers are very foolish to deliver them at that price; and if they have co-operative organizations in those areas operating in competition with the ordinary dealers they will not do so. The farmers will simply say they will deliver their eggs to a co-operative, which in turn utilizes the provisions of this act which will guarantee a price based on 38 cents. That would certainly be much higher than 26 to 28 cents in that area.

Supply-Agriculture
But we do not try to prosecute people for not doing that. We do not put the kind of teeth in the act the hon. member for Assini-boia asks us to put in it and prosecute people for not doing that. The chief reason we do not is that we could not prosecute them even if we had that kind of teeth there. That is a provincial authority and the courts can tell us we have no right to pass or enforce such law. The eggs are gathered in that area, and instead of being shipped directly to Toronto they are shipped in the opposite direction and then taken back to Toronto later. After they have gathered together a carload or whatever they want to ship they take them back to Toronto, deal directly with the merchant, supply him with eggs and he sells them to the public.
There are a lot of things that have to be done by the individuals concerned, both consumers and producers, if they want a different price for the eggs to the producer and perhaps a more reasonable price to the consumer, but they are not things we can do under this act, or on intraprovincial transactions under any act.
Mr. Chairman, I have been listening to farmers for quite a long while, and I was just wondering why they blame the government for not doing anything for them.
That is right.
I ask the minister if this $8 million is not the taxpayers' money and a subsidy to help the farmers to produce eggs on their farms. It is really a subsidy and goes to them.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: A wonderful gift!
There is a leading question. How about an answer?

I think the hon. member for Fort William is under a very great misapprehension when he mentions a figure of $8 million. I do not know where he grabbed that figure, but certainly it is not in the estimates book.
The minister seemed very surprised that we should be asking the government to get in the egg business. We have never asked the government to get in the egg business. The government has been saying for years that it has been in the egg business. It has just been a sham so far as the egg producers of the country are concerned, making them believe there is a floor price under eggs when in fact the government has not put a floor price under eggs at all. The secret has just come out now.

Oh, no.
tMr. Gardiner.]

The secret has come out. Why do you not tell the people what you are actually doing instead of leading them to believe you are protecting eggs with a support price under them? You have been carrying on this sham for quite some time.
Are you asking us to take it off altogether?

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: It is no good.
If you are not going to do any more than this, you might as well take it off.
No egg producer will agree with you.

What good is it to the producer? I asked the minister a question a minute ago and he still has not answered it. He said if the dealer bought them for 26 or 28 cents a dozen in the Lindsay district the government would not take them over.
Which?
If the dealer bought them for 26 or 28 cents a dozen in the Oshawa district, I think the minister said-
I said the district in between Toronto and Lindsay.

The minister said they would not buy the eggs because not enough had been paid for them, but the minister still has not answered the question I asked about the price to the producer. You said you had nothing to do with the eggs. In effect you are telling the producers that you have nothing to do with their eggs. You let the dealers go out and buy them as cheaply as they can.
We are not doing any such thing.
You have just said that.
I did not say that.
You just said it.

I did not say any such thing. I have explained three or four times already that there is no way of knowing what the price of the eggs should be unless you know where they pick them up, and if they have picked them up at such low prices they are not going to come to us in order to ask us to take them. There is no way of our getting that information. There is nobody who can compel them to pay that price except the provincial government, and they have not done so. They may think that is the better way of handling the situation.
I am not criticizing them. I am simply saying that is the fact. If the eggs were picked up at 26 cents a dozen at some point between the two places I have mentioned,

we would have to know whether it was necessary to take them all the way back to Lindsay and then cart them all the way from Lindsay to Toronto to know whether we should allow that as a deduction off the price the individual should get for the eggs. But the fact that they do not bring them to us at all pretty well indicates that they know we would not take them because they did not pay the producer enough, or that they have a good sale for them without bringing them to us at all; and that good sale is in Toronto, where they can sell at a price which gives them a high profit on the price they paid for them. Therefore they do not come near us at all and there is no provincial law or board which offers the farmer a competitive market.
I repeat that if we could compel them to deliver these eggs to us we could of course do some of the things we are being asked to do, but there is no law of ours that will compel them to do it and the only way they can be compelled is by a provincial law. If the province do not want to do that it is their affair, and they deal with their own people. Probably the people in your area should not elect you if you want a Conservative government to do that, because they have not done it.

We will leave that to the people of my district. The minister is now trying to place the blame on the provincial government. If that is the attitude the government is going to take, why do they not come out and say so-
You just said I did say so.
-instead of pretending they have a floor price under eggs?

Mr. Chairman, I want to stay with this matter of eggs for a moment. The hon. member for Assiniboia made specific reference to Brandon, and said that the price of eggs was particularly low there. I can confirm that bit of information from letters I have received from several farmers. For the past three months the price of A large has been 29 cents, A medium 21 cents and A small 17 cents. Can the minister explain the reason for the low prices received from dealers in the Brandon area?

The prices I quoted two days ago and which were referred to by the hon. member for Assiniboia were just the prices for one day, March 12, 1957, but the prices the hon. member has quoted as being in existence over a period are very close to the same thing. The prices given here for the one day to the producer at Brandon were 29 cents for A large, 24 cents 82715-160
