for A medium-you have 21, I think-and 18 cents for A small; I think your price was 17. The hon. member's prices applied averaged over a period. Apparently the prices I gave were on a day that was a little better so far as the medium and small grades were concerned.
All that demonstrates is that there is no one there who is taking these eggs and intending to deliver them to the board. At least if there is anyone they are not getting enough of the eggs to have the price any higher than that. That does not mean, though, that they could not take them there. They can take them there; but if there is any good reason for not taking them there, such as not being properly graded at grading stations and so on, they are not able to put them in.
I said Monday in a rather quick reply to the hon. member for Moose Mountain that probably most of them came from his constituency, or something to that effect. As he knows and I know, all the railroads out of his constituency run into Brandon. There is no doubt that eggs are accumulated in Brandon that come from Moose Mountain as well as the area that is tributary to Brandon in Manitoba; and possibly the number of eggs that accumulate there has something to do with the price, which is 1 cent lower than in Winnipeg.
The minister says the eggs should be delivered to the board in order to realize the higher price. Where should they be delivered in order to get them into the hands of the board?

They have to be delivered at a storage which is recognized as a proper storage. I imagine there should be storage in Brandon. I am not sure about that. I would think the packing plant there probably takes in eggs. But there is certainly plenty of storage in Winnipeg, and the eggs can be shipped there by anyone as long as they are in the quantities required, approximately a carload.

I think the Minister of Agriculture is a past master in hooking red herrings and dragging them across an issue in this chamber. We have been trying to get facts in respect to the federal government support price for eggs. The minister has said he has not received undue criticism. My experience is this, Mr. Chairman. Since I have been in parliament, going back to the first time this program was put into effect, farm organizations right across Canada, not only in Saskatchewan, have been sending petition after petition to this government to do something about the

Supply-Agriculture
federal act by which the producer will be able to benefit under this act rather than the processor.
I think there are a number of things we should clear up. Certainly the farm organizations even at this point have been asking for something to be done so the producer will get the benefit of the price support. I have here the memorandum which was placed before the government by the interprovincial farm union council in December, 1956. It states:
Surely such glaring differences in price between various grades throughout the marketing centres of Canada do not suggest the existence of an orderly egg marketing system.
Then it goes on to point out that something needs to be done in reference to the act. The other day the minister pointed out, I think quite inaccurately, or tried to leave the impression that Saskatchewan was the point where the producers were getting lower prices for their eggs than were being obtained at any other point in Canada. Then he tried to leave the impression that some lack of policy on the part of that provincial government was responsible for that situation. But then he went on to give the prices in various cities throughout Canada.
Which refutes just what you are saying.

It is
interesting to note that the prices in four cities in Saskatchewan were higher than they were in Brandon.
Under a Liberal government.

As
reported at page 2446 of Hansard the minister said this in respect to the setting up of cold storage plants in the various provinces:
The prices are pretty much in line with what the conditions under which delivery has to be made make necessary. The government that has been in power in Saskatchewan for 13 years has never built a storage for eggs and they were going to build everything. Those eggs have to be shipped to Winnipeg for storage, or shipped to Calgary in the other direction.
I should like to point out that he has now indicated to the house that egg prices in other parts of Canada, even in Brandon where these eggs are shipped, are lower than they are at points in Saskatchewan. I think the minister will agree when I say that I do not think there is a provincial government in Canada that has set up provincial storage plants. They have been set up with some assistance by the federal government, by private companies throughout the country.
The discrepancy between prices throughout the country indicates what we and other

members have been fighting for and have been trying to get the minister and the government to take cognizance of, namely the disparity between certain grades and prices.
I have here the source of the poultry products marketing report for August 31 through to November, and here is an indication showing the disparity between the prices and grades of eggs, showing that the producer is not getting a fair deal. At Calgary on August 28, 1956, just last fall, there was a 4-cent spread between grade A large and grade A medium, and 17 cents at Toronto on the same date. The difference between grade A medium and grade B at Calgary and Montreal was 2 cents at Montreal and 20 cents at Calgary.
What is the date, please?

This was August 28, 1956.
So, Mr. Chairman, the producers of eggs are trying to get orderly marketing and fair prices to the producer. I want to point out to the minister that if his government would undertake to pay the producer a price which would reflect the support price to the processor or the packer, then I think everyone would be satisfied.
I should like to point out to him that I think there is a simple method by which it can be done. I do not agree with him that there are not egg candling plants throughout a province like Saskatchewan, because there are. There are a great number of egg candling stations throughout Saskatchewan. The point is this. When the producer brings these eggs to market and they are shipped to any point-whether it is Winnipeg, Brandon, or any other point-there is no payment which comes back to the producer. I have seen these eggs shipped to those cold storage plants, and at that point they are graded.
I think the minister will have to agree that at some point these eggs generally reach the cold storage plant. I am suggesting that the minister set up some scheme by which, when they reach these storage plants and are graded, the shipper-whether it is a storekeeper or a co-operative egg candling plant -receive a payment back so the producer can get the advantage of the support price.
I should like to point out to him that I was in a place where there had been a return. This merchant had received a number of crates of eggs and had shipped them to Winnipeg. They went to the packers. The return came back after the eggs were graded, but of course he just got a certain price. I feel there should be a method set up by which these eggs are graded, the price for the various grades of eggs would be paid

back to the producer, and the producer in the first instance could get an intermediate payment and then a secondary payment later on. The way it is now I do not believe the minister has any way of checking these eggs which are going into storage, in order to determine whether or not the producer has received 25 cents a dozen for grade A large eggs or 32 cents or 38 cents, which might be the support price.
I am equally sure the minister cannot determine whether or not there has been a fair spread between what he has tried to indicate to the committee and the cost of taking these eggs from the producers to the points of storage. I do not see how the minister, under the present set-up, can give the house that assurance. So I am saying that under the present plan we have no guarantee to the producer. I along with other members have been trying to get this point across to the minister for years.
I should like to point out that this report from the poultry products marketing source indicates that there was a sudden drop last fall in the price of eggs, namely 35 per cent, within a few short weeks; and furthermore that the farmer's share of the consumer dollar for grade A large eggs declined from 74 per cent in August to 65 per cent in November.
I should like to point out that the price the consumer is paying for eggs does not reflect what the producer is getting. When we see the discrepancy I have indicated of 14 cents a dozen between what the producer gets and what the consumer pays in retail stores, I think there is something drastically wrong and something should be done about it. If there are too many eggs going into storage I would suggest that there are ways and means by which the Canadian people could receive some advantage from this. I believe people in the low income brackets could benefit by having these surplus eggs made available to them. Plans have been undertaken in other countries, such as stamp programs, by means of which these eggs could be made available to low income groups.
If the minister is trying to intimate to this committee that the United States program was in any way a program which added incentive to increase production, then I should say one of the first things we should have is a floor price which would represent something near the cost of production to the producer. Second, if we want to assist the poultry industry of this country, then some program has to be evolved by which advantages will be given to the low income groups. I think it is wrong, Mr. Chairman, to powder these eggs or to store them for long periods so they would not be fit for human consumption in
Supply-Agriculture
this country. If this government has vision, then a plan can be evolved by which, if eggs are in surplus production, the people in the low income groups can have those eggs made available to them. If we were to help the people in the low income brackets of this country as we should, then this program would receive the support of all members in this house.
I should like to ask the minister certain questions, because I think there is a good deal of confusion remaining as a result of what the minister has said. I should like the minister to give us the number of dozen eggs in storage, say for the last four years, and the support price. I should like the minister to give us the amount of money spent each year on the support of eggs over the last five years. If he has that information by provinces I should like to get it by provinces. I should like also to get the price per dozen at which this amount works out. If the minister has the information I should like him to give the committee figures showing how many provincial governments own their own storage plants, because I think the inference has been left here that Saskatchewan has not followed out some of the requests of the federal government, or co-operated with them.
In conclusion I might say that I am very happy to learn from the minister that we now have some hope of getting federal legislation by which the products marketing act will be amended so we can set up a provincial marketing board which will have authority to deal more effectively with producers' problems. I think this government has been remiss in allowing the years to slip by and trying to blame someone else for the problems. This afternoon the minister has pretty well gone the rounds in trying to blame someone else rather than accepting the responsibility which I think should be placed on the doorstep of the federal government. I do not believe the provincial governments are in a position, either constitutionally or in any other way, to meet these problems unless there is legislation which will provide for eggs and other commodities going into interprovincial or export trade.
In addition, I should point out to the minister and to the committee we have in Saskatchewan, as I think in most provinces, a natural products marketing act by means of which any producer group or co-operative can set up their own producer marketing scheme to come under federal legislation which this government might propose. I do hope that before we leave this item the minister can give some further assurance that he now knows the producers' problems; that he knows those of us who have been bringing these matters to his attention are interested in only

Supply-Agriculture
one thing. We feel that when we are spending public money, and there is a definite purpose for it, then it should be spent to meet that purpose. In this case the minister has indicated that it is to help the producer, but we say the price support act has not functioned in that way to date. I hope this new concept the government has will do that very thing.

I am not prepared to let this item go by without saying something about egg marketing. I listened with a great deal of interest the other night during the discussion of the floor price on cheese and again today regarding eggs. It was rather obvious that what I have said for many years is all too true, namely that the real purpose behind the Agricultural Prices Support Act has been to win two or three elections and not to support the prices of farm products, as the people of the country were led to believe it would.
In so far as eggs are concerned, it seems to me that whenever the minister gets in difficulties he blames it on the provinces. So long as everything is going along well he is quite prepared to take the credit. It does seem to me it should be possible, if the government were half as bright as they would like the people to believe, to frame some legislation whereby the producers would be guaranteed a floor price, instead of passing the responsibility on to the provinces. The government claims the credit when times are good. I think the best solution of the whole problem is to get rid of this government and start fresh next June.

All I would say with regard to that is the last time we did it eggs went down to 5 cents a dozen.
In answer to the questions asked by the hon. member for Moose Mountain, I would say I have not the figures in the form in which they have been requested. In the year 1950 we did not take any eggs at all. None were offered to us. In 1951 those that were offered to us only cost us $1,866.24, so there were not very many that year either. In 1952 it cost us $63,542.45 to pay for any losses we took on eggs which were turned over to us. In 1953 there were none at all. I am probably not exactly correct in saying there were none that were made available to us, but there were none turned over when we got to the period when eggs were to be taken.
Then in 1954 it cost us $546,268.87. During that summer eggs were as high as 85 cents a dozen. One of the reasons was that we had taken 107,000 cases of eggs off the market. As of July 1 we had agreed to accept those

eggs if they were turned over to us on December 1. They were held off the market until December 1, and eggs went as high as 85 cents to the consumer. It does not make any difference how anxious we are to help the producer, that kind of policy cannot be continued in a country where there are many more consumers than producers; and without provincial support in the form of legislation we cannot immediately deal with such conditions.

Why
did you allow it?

Why did we allow it? How are you going to stop it? If we do not have provincial legislation we cannot prevent eggs selling in Toronto at 85 cents which were bought from the farmer at 38 cents, but the provincial governments can do something about it in spite of what my hon. friends are saying; and that is the position.
We did do something about it, however. As a matter of fact I left the vacation I was taking at the farm out in Saskatchewan to come down here to see that something was done about it. We went to Toronto and into the chain stores and discussed the matter. I have already told the house about this two or three times, but apparently it does not register. We sent a man to Toronto who went and sat in with the chain stores and asked them why stored eggs were being sold at 45 cents a dozen when fresh eggs were being sold at 85 cents on the same counter, and the answer we received was that they were stored eggs and the housewives did not want them.
We launched an advertising campaign in the press to indicate that stored eggs are just as good as fresh eggs, with the result that they sold the stored eggs; but that did not lower the price of the other eggs from 85 cents to anything more than approximately 70 cents.
We have gone through all those experiences. I could quote the prices for the year, but I do not have them here at the moment and I do not think this is the proper time to discuss that particular question anyway, because that can be done under the genera) estimates, at which time I will have all the information on hand.
The fact remains, however, that those eggs were handled in that way at that time As a result of their being handled in tha1 way we changed the regulations the nex1 year to provide that we would not take any eggs before July 1 that we were noable to put back on the market until, le' us say, December 1. We reserved the righ to put them on the market at any time. Sc if you took the average price for this las year in which they were able to do that yoi

would get a very high average through the summer months of the year; but when you come to the next year when the farmer was better dealt with, the average price to the consumer would be lower because at that time whenever anyone tried to run the price of eggs up to 85 cents we put eggs on the market.
Speaking from memory, I think at the present time we have something over 100,000 cases of eggs that are oil dipped, and if anyone attempts to sell eggs to the consumer at prices like those which prevailed in 1954 we will put those eggs on the market and get our money back as far as this fund is concerned. We will see to it that there is a proper relationship between the price the farmer is getting for the eggs and the price the consumer has to pay.
That is not a simple thing to do. It would be much simpler if we could draft legislation and send it down to any one of the provincial capitals where the trouble lies and get it passed, but we are not in a position to do that. But when they draft legislation and send it here somebody over in the C.C.F. group says we ought to pass it.
When did you send any legislation to a provincial government?
We did not send any; we have more sense than that. It is only my friends on the other side of the house who suggest we ought to do that.

You
have never invited any.

The suggestion is made that that is the way to deal with it. The way to deal with governments that refuse to do that kind of thing is for the people to vote them out. That is the democratic and constitutional way to do it, and no doubt in due course the people will get around to doing that even in Saskatchewan.

Has
the minister any suggestion to make to this committee about the kind of legislation we might have, let us say in the province of Saskatchewan? We have at the present time the natural products marketing board act under which any producer group has the privilege of setting up any type of marketing legislation it desires. I should like to know-

Let me answer that question before you ask so many that I forget it. I think that was included in the other one, and the answer is that the very people you are talking about in Saskatchewan in the last two or three weeks have been asking
Supply-Agriculture
for exactly what I am suggesting ought to be done respecting the egg marketing in the province of Saskatchewan and if the provincial government does not do it there is nothing we can do about it down here.

Mr. Chairman, what the minister has said is correct, in all probability, but no group of producers in the province of Saskatchewan to my knowledge have ever gone to a provincial government and asked for a marketing board and been denied. If they are now asking for this it may very well be that they realize they have to take further action in that regard; I cannot say. As far as I can see from the information the minister has given to the committee, if in 1954 the federal government spent-I think it was $546,000; is that correct?
Yes, that is correct.

And
if in 1953 they did not spend anything in price support, the only conclusion I can come to is that it is the fault of the administration of the minister's department, because since he saw fit to change the regulations in 1955 so these people could not have the advantage of using federal money and then held the eggs off the market, I think it is a clear indication that something could have been done by the government in 1954 to prevent that sort of thing.

Well, Mr. Chairman, of course anyone who has never had these things to do can easily talk about them, but there is no possible way for the government to guess what some people may do. As far as this situation is concerned both parties went ahead with their eyes wide open. If my hon. friend goes back and searches the record he will find there were a lot of people storing eggs in 1954 who had not been in the egg business prior to that time. In other words there are people who sit around watching for these things which are going on and who seek an opportunity of making a profit here and a profit there; and when they do they step into it. When we found that there were a number of those people who were turning eggs over to the government we did take action. It is true that it cost something to do so. In order to answer the question asked a few minutes ago I now have the figures concerning a number of cases of eggs. This year we have purchased 98,900 cases of eggs, and there are 30 dozen in every case. The number that are stored to specification is 57,088 cases. Those that are stored to specification are not sold outright to the government.

As a result of the action that was taken following the experience of 1954, we have 98,900 cases of eggs which we purchased. I want to stress again that we are concerned about the producer getting a reasonable price, and we look after that; but we are also concerned about the consumer having to pay anywhere from 70 to 85 cents a dozen for eggs that were bought from the farmer at these prices which some might consider to be reasonable.

So are
we concerned about it.

Mr. Chairman, I do not know how profitable it will be to continue this debate, because it seems to me there is a great deal of confusion in the minds of those on this side of the house, and every time the minister rises to his feet he compounds that confusion.
That is not my fault.
Oh, no?

When I say that I am thinking particularly of some of the arguments the minister put forward as to why the producer is not receiving a fair price.
I have in mind the argument he made on Monday last, when he pointed out that one province in particular had not provided cold storage facilities and therefore there was a difference of possibly 2 or 3 cents a dozen because the eggs had to be shipped to Winnipeg. That argument has been knocked sky-high by the figures the minister has placed on the record.
There has been quite a bit of speculation on the part of the minister that things would be considerably better if and when the provincial governments undertook to accept responsibility to the producers by placing legislation on their statute books which would facilitate the setting up of marketing boards. Within the last two or three days a delegation from Ontario has been here in Ottawa. Ontario has such legislation, but these people found that because of complications arising from interprovincial trade they must now come to the federal government and ask for federal legislation in order that their own legislation may mean something in so far as the producers are concerned.
The hon. member for Moose Mountain pointed out that he doubts if there is a province which has not some kind of marketing legislation, but because of interprovincial trade barriers the schemes mean little if anything to the producers. Apparently the minister is aware that something further could be done to help the producers, and being aware of that I would suggest that he

realize the time is long overdue when this government should accept its responsibilities and initiate federal legislation. The government could then go to the provinces and say, "We have done our part. It is now up to you to pass the necessary enabling legislation." This government must take the leadership in this matter.
I submit that there is only one man who should be supported, and that is the primary producer. What is the use of supporting the price to the packer? Experience has shown that whenever the packer is supported he finds many ways of seeing that the producer does not get his fair share. If he cannot do it by grading he does it in some other way. I do not care whether there is a government grader on the premises, that is what happens. I suggest that the government should initiate the necessary federal legislation and then go to the provinces and say, "Here is the legislation. You go ahead and introduce enabling legislation and show that you really want to do something for the producers of primary products."

Mr. Chairman, I should
like to obtain some information regarding a problem which I believe is of deep concern to the dairying industry in Canada. What is the attitude of the government with respect to the submission made by a number of dairy organizations that a new tariff schedule be established on cheese and powdered milk coming into this country? It is my understanding that they asked for a 4-cent tariff on powdered milk and a 6-cent tariff on cheese.

The position of the government is pretty well set out in what I read to the committee a few minutes ago, when I gave in substance the terms of the order in council dealing with powdered skim milk. However, this begins at a much earlier time. We are part of the commonwealth, and so are New Zealand and Australia. The climate in those countries is such that they can run their cattle outside the year round and their costs of production are quite low as compared with ours. They are thus able to produce milk products at lower prices and ship them here and undersell our product.
At one time there was a duty of 14 cents on butter, and as a result butter could not be imported into this country. However, representations were made by those two countries that they should be given a preference because they were part of the commonwealth and we should all be interested in helping one another. So the government of the day reduced the duty on butter to 5 cents in so far as those two countries were concerned. There was an understanding reached-I am

not going into the details-that there should be an agreement arrived at before butter was sent to this country. Some attempt was made to overcome that, and at one time the government of the day placed butter in bond and held it there until they had a written agreement from the country concerned. For a short time at the end of the war they seemed to forget that it was in existence and we did get a comparatively small amount of butter. But this arrangement has applied right through. I might mention that some few years ago the duty on butter was reduced to 12 cents a pound, but even this duty has been sufficient to keep out other butter.
In the case of cheese the duty is only 1 cent per pound from New Zealand or Australia, with a 7-cent duty under the general tariff which keeps out cheese from other countries, except the special kinds which sell at higher prices. In connection with Australia and New Zealand there is what I called the other day a gentleman's agreement which does not permit cheese to come here at all unless the consent of the Canadian government is given.
Until a few days ago it was open to Australia and New Zealand to ship powdered milk to Canada, or it was open to dealers in this country to obtain powdered milk from those countries. Representations were made that a 4-cent duty would stop that; that a 6-cent duty on cheese would stop that; and that a comparable duty on butter would do the same if the written agreement did not have that effect.
Before you can start to put a policy of that kind into effect there must be discussions and conferences, particularly with countries within the commonwealth. It was stated in the budget speech that some such conferences would be held dealing with these products. In the meantime cheese is taken care of, butter is taken care of and powdered milk is being taken care of. Yesterday we put a floor price on powdered milk, and we now have understandings with both these countries that they will not send any in without our consent.
But the main feature of the program in so far as the farm organizations are concerned is that the whole tariff matter will be under discussion. We could not take care of that in sufficient time to do anything about it at the present moment, so we are dealing with it in the other way. We think it will be just as effective for the time being as it would be if a tariff were imposed.

Mr. Chairman, I did not want to let this opportunity pass without saying something further about the minister's reference to 1930 and 1935. I think if hon. members will take a look at the figures they will agree that while some farmers may have got only 5 cents a dozen for their eggs, that 5 cents would buy more at that time than the price being received now will purchase today. This is the result of the inflation that has gone on under this government.
Furthermore, the farmers got into that fix because of the administration during the previous years when the Liberal government was in power. It was only our coming to power, and Mr. Bennett bringing in his national products marketing act, that brought some relief. It is true the act was found to be ultra vires, but it was probably the best marketing legislation which had been introduced to that time.
Due to the findings of the supreme court, farmers' organizations of all kinds are now asking that the legislation be amended, and I hope amendments will be brought in this session so no further delay will be caused, and so the manufacturers and packers may not be able to take advantage of a disorganized marketing system to further gouge the producer.
I want to say also that during the eleven months of 1956 specified in a return tabled under my name very recently, 3,500,000 dozen eggs, or their equivalent in powdered and processed form, were imported into this country. In this case, as in a good many others of a similar kind, the ground is being cut right out from under the feet of the Canadian farmer and producer. Over the years you have been able to fool the farmers, but you still have the packers as your friends, and that is the reason these things are done.

Mr. Chairman, I have been listening to the discussion with a great deal of interest, and I thought the minister was almost at the point of giving us some specific information. At least I am going to give him an opportunity of doing so now.
The minister stated on a number of occasions in relation to the marketing of eggs that the provinces had a certain responsibility to provide the kind of legislation-I think I heard him correctly-which would result in the producer getting his fair share of the support price now paid under the guarantee to the dealer or the packer. But at no point to my knowledge, and I have read his remarks carefully, did he indicate just what kind of legislation that would be. It is probably a matter of opinion, but perhaps I could put it this way. Can the minister say if there is

Supply-Agriculture
any province in Canada which at the present time has the type of legislation with regard to the marketing of eggs which, in his opinion, would bring to the producer, or help bring to the producer, a fair share of the guaranteed price of eggs?

All the provinces have legislation with regard to dairy products which do that very thing, and there was just as much discussion about it then as there is today about eggs. The hon. member may not remember; probably he is not old enough, I do not know. He may not remember the days when they used to have cream cans inside every store. A chap came along with a quart jar of cream, poured it in and credited it to his account at the store. These cream accounts were a common thing, and there was a lot of complaint about the kind of butter that was made from the cream so collected.
But they did bring in an act. I think the first province that brought one in was Saskatchewan, and that was as much an election issue as the hon. members are trying to make of eggs now. But it was not the federal government who looked after it; it was the provincial government. They put in grading stations, and said the product had to be up to certain standards. Then later on they refused to let them handle it in the old way in the stores at all. Cream of proper quality had to be delivered to the creameries, and finally they reached the point where, in the province of Saskatchewan, they were able to produce some of the best butter made in Canada.
The same thing can be done with regard to eggs, but you have to start in the provinces because there are far more eggs sold inside the provinces, eggs which are produced in the provinces, than are exported outside. It is not a fair comparison to start comparing wheat marketing with eggs, as the hon. member for Assiniboia did. Wheat, in the first place, is not a perishable product. In the second place between 70 and 80 per cent of it is sold outside the country. The law with regard to it has always been questionable in the minds of legal people, but no one will test the law because it would not be in the interests of any one group to do so. So they say anyone who puts up an elevator to handle wheat is operating in the national interest. But try to do it in the case of eggs and see where you will end up. You would have consumers throwing them at you before long.
The handling of eggs is an entirely different matter. Eggs are breakable, perishable to the highest degree; they are marketed at a great many places, and many of them never get out of the community in which they are

marketed. In most of the towns in Saskatchewan, as a matter of fact-it used to be true all over the country and to some extent, no doubt, it is still true-merchants took the eggs at a certain price and sold them to the people in the community for the same price. In other words they were merely a medium of exchange between the people who raised them in the country and the people who consumed them in the town or village. If they had a few to send out they sent them out, but to say that this is setting the price of eggs is drawing the thing a little fine. When you want to produce eggs, say, in Saskatchewan to ship to Toronto, then they must be properly graded because they will be coming into competition with eggs produced in that province. So they must be properly packed and shipped so as to reach the market in proper condition.
The provinces all know this. We have a discussion similar to this in the first week in December every year, and all the provincial governments are represented. The method of putting this into effect is well known throughout the length and breadth of the country, and the people who went back from the last meeting that was held-organized in Saskatchewan-went right to the government. When the hon. member says it was never tried before, his memory is not very good. It is not very many years since the egg producers in Saskatchewan attempted to organize a board to handle their eggs, but after some experience in the matter they dropped it. Now they are trying it again, and no doubt if the proper educational campaign is carried on, if my hon. friends will co-operate with me and tell them how to do it in the campaign that lies ahead, then I am sure it will be done before we enter upon a new session of the house.

I want to thank the minister for the lecture he has given us on the difference between eggs and wheat. I appreciate that there are those differences. But the question I asked was not answered, except by inference, and the only inference I can draw is that no province has the type of legislation with regard to the marketing of eggs which the minister has in mind. He did not state exactly what he had in mind. One of the reasons I raise this matter is that in all the replies the minister has made on this question over a period of months he has been picking on the province of Saskatchewan and blaming that province

That is because you are
starting all the talking over there.

As the minister knows, I am not speaking for the province of Saskatchewan, but it seems to me there is a bit of unfairness in the minister's attitude. He went

so far today as to say that if the government of the province of Saskatchewan was not doing the things it ought to be doing, then it should be voted out.
In the province of Manitoba, where we have a sort of Liberal government, a hybrid of a type-they do not admit being purely Liberal, but it is the closest thing to a Liberal government-they do not have this type of legislation that the minister seems to think should exist. Is the minister going to say that the people of the province of Manitoba should vote out that government? Apparently they will have the opportunity to do so very soon, much sooner than the people of Saskatchewan, who have just gone through an election. I do not think this kind of question should be dealt with on that sort of basis. We are not attempting to place eggs on the political market here.
Oh, no.

We are trying to find a way by which the producer of eggs can be guaranteed that he is going to get his fair share of the guaranteed price under the Agricultural Prices Support Act, and the minister himself admits that has not taken place up to the present time. The figures he has placed on the record only today indicate that the intermediaries, the packing houses and other individuals, he said-I do not know what he meant by it-have been taking advantage of the act for their own benefit and have not been passing on the benefit of the support price to the producer.
That is exactly what my colleague the hon. member for Moose Mountain and others of this group have been telling the minister for the last 18 months, and at last he has come around to admitting it. But this is not the point at which to start a political wrangle. This is the point at which the minister can do a service to the egg producers of this country if he can set out in clear-cut terms what in his opinion should be done. After all, he has the staff in his department to get the information for him. They have had experience with the act. The minister has the agricultural prices support board from which he can get advice.
The minister says he is going to give certain advice very soon during an election campaign. In my opinion the worst possible place to hand out advice about marketing legislation is from a platform during an election campaign, because it will be confused by a dozen other things that do not belong in the same discussion. We are now talking about a specific thing. The minister has an opportunity to do a great service to the egg producers by placing a plan before the house. We do not expect him to be infallible, and 82715-161
Supply-Agriculture
it may not be the best plan in the world; but at least he should suggest something so the provinces can pass the proper type of legislation. The problem is common to all provinces. Then with the federal government playing its support role and placing a floor price under eggs the situation can be resolved.
At the present time, however, I think the minister has left the question pretty well up in the air, if I may say so, because instead of stating clearly what in his opinion the provinces could do he keeps repeating that if the provinces were to carry out their responsibilities the situation would be different. Even if we agree with that, what in his opinion is it that the provinces are supposed to do in order to remedy the situation? I think that is the real question.
I do not wish to prolong the discussion at all. I have not even taken part until now, but if the minister is going to go to the extent of placing all the blame on one province and advocating that the people of that province should vote out the government, we are going to have a political discussion and it is going to be a long and bitter one. I am leaving it open for the minister, if he wishes to do so, to lay a plan before the committee; or if he would rather communicate directly with the provinces that will be fine. I hope he is not planning to carry this matter into the political arena and start the egg-throwing contest which he mentioned a while ago.

Mr. Chairman, I have placed it before the house at every session for the last six years, and it will only take a minute to lay it before this house again this session. Every province understands what could be done. We have set a floor under eggs, in spite of what my hon. friend says, and that floor is 38 cents basis storage plant. Any persons who understand the situation and are trying to work under it can work out what the price ought to be.
For example, when eggs were being picked up at very low prices in the area south of Swift Current we set the price at 27 cents for grade A large eggs, and we bought them at that price. That was the first time we did buy eggs in the intermediate season. We said that the proper price for eggs at that point was 27 cents and that we would buy them there, and we did buy them there. They would have been 29 cents or 30 cents if it had not been for the fact that we had to ship them either to Winnipeg or Calgary after buying them. So the price might have been set by someone as high as 30 cents, but we could not say that the price of eggs was 30 cents.
Having established a position where no one who did that was going to take any loss, the provincial government could say that the

Supply-Agriculture
price of eggs in Swift Current is 30 cents or if, to be absolutely safe, they preferred to make it 27 they could say 27, and they could say that anyone who bought grade A large eggs at any price lower than that was breaking the law. They can say that. We cannot say that. If that were said it would immediately set a basis on which the price would operate in that province, but it would not operate on nest run eggs, on eggs that were cracked or on B eggs that have to be broken. There would have to be somewhat different prices set for those eggs in order to bring that about.
The provincial government can do that, but we are not able to. You can enlarge on that to your heart's content, but it is a system that everybody understands whether they are in provincial or federal politics.

I thank the minister for that statement. I want to ask one more question. Suppose in any particular province an egg marketing board were set up which undertook to do exactly what the minister has outlined, set a price at which they would be prepared to buy eggs in that province. Would the minister's department then be in a position to guarantee to that board any losses they might sustain as between the price they had to pay and the price at which they had to dispose of the eggs?

We would take over all the eggs from the board that they wanted to hand over to us at the end of a season or during a season when they were in storage. We would take them over at 38 cents plus carrying charges, which might mean as high as 42 cents. I think at present it is 43 cents. That is what I mean by saying there is no possibility of their taking any loss. The loss, if there is any, is borne by this act. They could turn those eggs over to us just as dealers can turn them over now.
The board would get their eggs from farmers and dealers all over the place. They would sell whatever they could, and if they could sell them on the market at higher prices they would not come near us. They would do exactly the same thing as those who are handling eggs now have been accused of doing. There is nothing to prevent them selling them at a higher price than they pay for them, but when it gets to the point where they cannot sell them to anyone else they can sell them to the agricultural prices support board on the basis of 38 cents at storage, and the board is responsible for marketing them from then on. By saying that the provinces must co-operate we simply mean that if we are going to make the act operate successfully everywhere the provinces must come in and state what the price is.

Mr. Chairman, the minister
says on the one hand that the farm organizations are pretty well satisfied with the operations of the act.

I did intend to enlarge on that and say that since they made their recommendations last fall we have made certain changes, and we have bought 98,900 cases of eggs. We had never done that before until they brought in their suggestions that changes should be made. We did make certain changes, and we are buying eggs now all through the season.

I think the recommendations made by the farm organizations have not been fully complied with, even in the light of the statement the minister has now made. It is probably true that in order to make the act as effective as possible there needs to be certain complementary legislation on the statute books of the various provinces. It would seem to me that the best type of legislation might be that which would delegate authority under this act and also under any provincial act to certain co-operative marketing organizations composed of producers. But until such time as the minister and the federal government are prepared to see that their floor prices are passed on to the producer at least to the extent of being paid on any eggs going into interprovincial trade, it seems to me that it is placing any single province almost in an impossible position to suggest that any legislation they might place on their own statute books would in fact make this legislation completely operative. It has not provided floor prices to the producer. The government has merely said that it is prepared to buy at certain prices eggs that go into storage.
The minister has told us that grade A medium eggs have varying spreads at different times, and that the prices support board has been unable to set a price for grade A medium eggs to prevent this very huge spread. If that is correct, it seems to me that the agricultural prices support board is going backward, because in 1949-50 they set a price for grade A medium eggs of 36 cents a dozen, which was just 2 cents below the 38 cents per dozen price for grade A large eggs. If that kind of action was taken back in 1949, it would seem to me that in 1957 they should be doing at least as much as they were doing in that earlier period to see that there is not an undue spread between the price of grade A large eggs and grade A medium eggs.
The floor price of 38 cents a dozen was first set, I believe, for the year 1949-50. Since that time the floor price has remained the same. But since 1949 the cost of production

in the country has gone up by a very substantial amount. In 1949 the index of farm costs was 204 and in August of last year the index of costs was 254 or an increase in the cost of production of about 25 per cent over that period. So while the government floor price on eggs has remained in cents the same, the price has been steadily getting lower in real terms because of the ever-increasing cost of production.
The farm organizations are not satisfied with the government's legislation. The farm organizations, including the farmers' union and the federation of agriculture, believe the legislation is defective and should be changed. The interprovincial farm union council, in their memorandum to the federal-provincial agricultural conference in December of last year, recommend that the floor price on eggs of 38 cents per dozen for grade A large be a direct guarantee to the producer instead of to the wholesaler as at present. They made a number of recommendations in connection with the poultry industry, but that was their main recommendation as far as this legislation is concerned.
The minister referred to the advisory committee to the agricultural prices support board. He referred to the Canadian Federation of Agriculture and their attitude to the government's legislation. I have in my hand the annual presentation by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture to the Prime Minister of Canada and members of the cabinet, Ottawa, February 15, 1957. In it they make a direct reference to the Agricultural Prices Support Act by saying this:
There is no doubt that the Agricultural Prices Support Act, together with the operation of the Canadian wheat board on its present basis, has in the past few years protected agriculture from some of the worst of the price collapses to which it would otherwise have been subject.
The orderly marketing program in butter, and the other applications of the government's powers under the act in eggs, hogs, dry skim milk and other products have all been of value. At the same time we think it must be conceded that as it has developed over the years the policy and philosophy of the government in the administration of this act has been in most respects that the support board program should be a minimum one, available only in cases of extreme price decline and in circumstances where the cost to the government would be moderate and the possibility of creating any real problems in the fields of surplus disposal and trade relations almost entirely avoided.
Further on they say this:
After seeing it in operation for some time the members of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture have arrived at the conclusion that the support board's program as it is now carried on does not represent a sufficiently determined effort to achieve the purpose of the prices support act, which is that "the board shall endeavour to secure a fair relationship between the returns from agriculture and 82715-161J
Supply-Agriculture
those from other industries". We therefore suggest that a greater use be made, in the future, of the Agricultural Prices Support Act as a means of maintaining adequate market support prices of those farm commodities to which the act applies. Eggs, fowl and turkeys provide immediate opportunities for the application of this request.
That is a clear statement from the Canadian Federation of Agriculture-
And this is clear action.

-that the act as it is at present being operated is insufficient, and that the whole attitude and philosophy of the government and of the board toward price support for farm products is inadequate and does not meet present conditions. As they have explained, the attitude of the government today is a very minimum amount of price supports for agricultural products. They say that while the act has been of some real value, it has not maintained a fair income for agricultural producers generally but has merely prevented a very drastic collapse at a given time in the prices of certain agricultural commodities.
We have had this discussion this afternoon because the prices of eggs have been so low at so many dates in recent times. Generally speaking I think it is fair to say that agricultural prices in recent months have been extremely low. They have been extremely low in relation to the farmer's cost of production. I was amazed the other night to hear the Minister of Finance say that the major factor in the increase in the consumer price index was the recovery of agricultural and food prices. I do not believe the major cause of inflation to the consumer has been a recovery in the last year in agricultural prices. I do not think that is correct. I do not think it is a statement of fact.
It may be true, and I have no doubt that it is true, that the food component of the consumer price index has increased perhaps more than any other component. But it is a great deal different to say that has been the case-which is the retail price of food and not the price to the producer- and to say that the major factor in the increase in the consumer price index was the recovery of agricultural and food prices; because if the recovery of agricultural food prices means anything, it means the recovery to the producer.

Let me at once say that I was referring to the index and the components of the index. I was not having anything to say about the return to the farmer.

I am glad to hear the minister make that correction or that amendment, because I think it is an extremely important one.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It is not important at all. It is just that my hon. friend chose to read into my remarks things I did not say.
No, I did not. I merely quoted your words which were as follows: "The major factor in the increase in the consumer price index was the recovery of agricultural and food prices".

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is correct.

Not to the producer. If an agricultural price means anything it is a price to the agricultural industry. It is surely not a price to Loblaws and all the huge chain stores that are setting up shopping centres and asking the consumer to pay for them by very high food prices. Of course that statement by the minister was fully in keeping with the statement made just before, that if everything went well the farmers would have a higher income in 1957 than they had in 1951.
The thing we have been trying to get across to the government for a long time now is that the agricultural industry is in a bad way; that prices paid to farmers are inadequate; that the farmers across this nation by the thousands are going broke and going out of business; that they are caught in a price-cost squeeze, and that their prices have been remaining almost the same for the past few years while the costs of production have been going up. I think whenever the government or any minister is referring to agricultural prices as a component part of the consumer index he should make it quite clear that the producer is not receiving any substantial part of the increase in retail food prices. As a matter of fact, for a number of years now the producers' percentage of the retail food dollar has been going down. The prices of food go up and the payments to the producers remain the same or, in fact, decrease.
I suggest that the stand taken by the farmers' union, and the stand taken by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, is a stand in keeping with the thinking of the agricultural producers of this nation, namely that the government's Agricultural Prices Support Act is inadequate; that it is being inefficiently administered; that the benefits paid for by the taxpayers are not flowing to the producer as they should.

I should like one further word on this matter. I think it was P. T. Barnum who said there is always a gimmick. I was very interested in the minister's statement

a moment ago in which he put forward a concise plan by which the provinces could set up producers' boards that would give the farmers, in this case for eggs, a reasonable price. I do not want to put words in the minister's mouth-
You will do that anyway, whether or not you want to.

I suggest he said this, that in the case of Saskatchewan that province could set up a board and pay the producer say 35 cents a dozen for eggs, and that his board would take the eggs off their hands at 38 cents plus any carrying charges
I did not say 35 cents.
No, you did not say 35 cents.
You are putting words in my mouth.

Any price; 27 cents, then. Can you imagine, Mr. Chairman, what would happen to a provincial board which undertook to pay a price like that? People bordering the province would come into the province and would completely wreck any hope the board had of carrying out the job it intended to do. Certainly that is no solution, and the minister knows such a plan would never succeed under those circumstances.
We listened to the same arguments when we acted on dairy products.
